source_refs.note: Exercise 3.5, Question 11: show-that using an odd integrand on [-1, 1]; book p. 102. No printed answer (show that).

blocks.explanation:
A proof on the symmetric interval \([-1, 1]\).
Split \((1 - x)f(1 - x^2)\) into \(f(1 - x^2) - x f(1 - x^2)\); the second piece is odd, so its integral is 0 (Property V).
What is left is the right side.
steps:
Given: any continuous \(f\).
To prove: \(\int_{-1}^{1} (1 - x)f(1 - x^2)\,dx = \int_{-1}^{1} f(1 - x^2)\,dx\).
Method: Property IX to split, then Property V (odd function on \([-a, a]\)).

Split the integral
\[\int_{-1}^{1} (1 - x)f(1 - x^2)\,dx\]
\[= \int_{-1}^{1} f(1 - x^2)\,dx - \int_{-1}^{1} x f(1 - x^2)\,dx\]
Why: multiply out \((1 - x)\) and use Property IX.

The second integrand is odd
\[h(x) = x f(1 - x^2)\]
\[h(-x) = (-x)f\big(1 - (-x)^2\big)\]
\[= -x f(1 - x^2) = -h(x)\]
Why: \((-x)^2 = x^2\), so \(f(1 - x^2)\) does not change, while the factor \(x\) changes sign.

Apply Property V
\[\int_{-1}^{1} x f(1 - x^2)\,dx = 0\]
\[\int_{-1}^{1} (1 - x)f(1 - x^2)\,dx = \int_{-1}^{1} f(1 - x^2)\,dx\]
Why: the integral of an odd function over \([-a, a]\) is 0.

Check with an example
\[f(u) = u:\ \int_{-1}^{1} (1 - x)(1 - x^2)\,dx = \dfrac{4}{3}\]
\[\int_{-1}^{1} (1 - x^2)\,dx = \dfrac{4}{3} \;\checkmark\]
Why: the extra part \(-\int_{-1}^{1} x(1 - x^2)\,dx\) is 0 because \(x - x^3\) is odd.
